715.title: The Song of Deborah (Judges 5:1–12)
715.hook: the war is sung again, and she calls herself "a mother in Israel"
715.howItsDone: The Song of Deborah is read in synagogue as the haftarah on the Shabbat when the Song at the Sea, Exodus 15, is read from the Torah, known as Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jael, at her tent door, where the war ended. Your line was blessed in the tent. Did you thank someone underestimated? Today, the same story again, as a song. Day seven hundred fifteen.

For a while, nobody used the main roads. Travelers took the back paths. Village life stopped. That's how the song remembers the bad years, and it's a picture anyone who has lived through a frightening time might recognize: empty streets, people keeping out of sight, everyone going the long way round. Chapter four told the war as a story. Chapter five tells it again, and this time it's sung. It opens: "Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day."
screen: `NOBODY USED THE MAIN ROADS.` → `CHAPTER FOUR TOLD IT; CHAPTER FIVE SINGS IT.` → `THEN SANG DEBORAH AND BARAK.`

segments.voice: The song doesn't begin with the battle. It begins with the people who showed up. Praise the Lord, it says, when the people offered themselves willingly. Then it calls out to kings and princes: listen. I will sing to the Lord. And before any fighting, it remembers the God of Sinai, when the earth trembled and the mountains flowed. Then it names the emptiness: the roads abandoned, the villages emptied, until, Deborah sings, "I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel." A mother in Israel. Not a commander, not a queen, not even a judge, though she was one. She chooses a word from home. Some readers hear in it a whole idea of leadership: care before command, someone who notices who's missing and gets people back on the roads. The song keeps widening the circle. It blesses the leaders who volunteered. It calls to people who ride, people who sit in judgment, people who walk by the way. It imagines the victory being retold at the places where people draw water, the ordinary gathering spots, so the good news travels by word of mouth. And then the song turns on itself: "Awake, awake, Deborah: awake, awake, utter a song." Even the singer has to be told to wake up and sing. Rescue isn't finished, the song suggests, until someone remembers it out loud, together, and gives it a tune.
screen: `PRAISE FOR THE PEOPLE WHO SHOWED UP.` · `THE ROADS EMPTY, UNTIL I AROSE.` · `A MOTHER, NOT A COMMANDER.` · then, large: `AWAKE, AWAKE, UTTER A SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing about something that went right. Bring to mind one thing that worked out lately: a hard day you got through, a recovery, a kindness that arrived on time, a problem solved. Remember the people who showed up for it. Then give it a sound. Hum a tune you know, or say the thing slowly with a little rhythm, the way the song turns news into music. No one needs to hear it but you. If you like, borrow the song's own words for it: awake, awake, utter a song. The bell holds the time.
Awake. The command the Song of Deborah gives itself, waking the singer up to tell the victory out loud. Today's word.
Your line: a mother in israel. Today, tell someone the story of one thing that went right, and name who showed up for it. Day seven hundred fifteen.

screen: `DAY 715 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SISERA'S MOTHER AT THE WINDOW.`

716.title: Sisera's mother at the window (Judges 5:28–30)
716.hook: the song pauses on the enemy's mother, waiting; later tradition hears her cries in the shofar's notes
716.howItsDone: Jews read Sisera's mother in the Song of Deborah, and the Talmud's discussion of the shofar's teruah sound in tractate Rosh Hashanah draws on the verse about her crying, a link remembered when the shofar is blown on Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Deborah, which told itself to awake, and a leader who called herself a mother in Israel. Your line was a mother in israel. Did you tell the story of something that went right? Today, the song finds another mother. Day seven hundred sixteen.

Through a lattice, a woman watches an empty road. The song of victory has been loud: the stars fighting from their courses, the river sweeping the enemy away, Jael blessed in her tent. Then, near the very end, it goes quiet and moves somewhere unexpected. Not to Israel's camp. To the enemy's house. "The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?"
screen: `A WOMAN AT A LATTICE.` → `THE SONG GOES QUIET.` → `WHY IS HIS CHARIOT SO LONG IN COMING?`

segments.voice: We know something she doesn't. Her son is already dead, in a stranger's tent. She's still at the window. Her wisest ladies try to comfort her, and she answers herself with the same words: they must be dividing the spoil. A girl or two for every man. Dyed cloth for Sisera, embroidered on both sides, for the necks of the victors. The song doesn't make her innocent. Her comfort is plunder, and captive women from someone else's town. She's imagining exactly the kind of victory her son had been winning over Israel. And still the song stays with her. It gives her the window, the lattice, the questions, the waiting. Then it ends with a line of its own: "So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD." The song holds both at once: a victory it celebrates, and a mother it can't stop looking at. Jewish tradition kept looking too. Remember teruah, the great shout at Jericho? It's also a shofar call. When the Talmud asks what the teruah of Rosh Hashanah should sound like, it reaches for this verse. The word for her crying, vateyabev, is the clue. The rabbis ask whether her cry was a groan or a sob, and the shofar sounds both. And later tradition hears her cries in the shofar's notes. On the day of judgment, in the middle of the new year's prayers, the sound that wakes the congregation carries the cry of the enemy's mother. Nobody has to excuse what her son did to remember that she waited at a window for someone who wasn't coming home.
screen: `WE KNOW WHAT SHE DOESN'T.` · `HER COMFORT IS PLUNDER.` · `THE SONG HOLDS BOTH.` · then, large: `HER CRY IN THE SHOFAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the other side's grief. Bring to mind someone on the other side of something: an argument you won, a rivalry, a team that lost, a group your people disagree with, a neighbor you're at odds with. You don't have to change your mind about anything. Just find the person at their window. Who is waiting for them? What might they be afraid of tonight? Let the picture stay for a moment, without excusing anything, and without looking away. The bell holds the time.
vateyabev. The cry of Sisera's mother at the window, waiting for a chariot that won't come, which tradition hears in the shofar. Today's word.
Your line: the other mother waits. Today, when you hear news of someone else's loss, stop for one breath and think of who is waiting for them. Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: Mighty, while hiding (Judges 6:11–16)
717.hook: the angel calls a frightened man threshing in secret "thou mighty man of valor"
717.howItsDone: Jews study the Gideon chapters as part of the Former Prophets, and rabbinic commentary often asks why a frightened man threshing in hiding was the one chosen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sisera's mother at the window, crying vateyabev, waiting for a son who wasn't coming home. Your line was the other mother waits. Did you remember someone's grief on the far side of a fight? Today, a new judge, found hiding. Day seven hundred seventeen.

Threshing is open-air work. You beat the grain on a flat floor, and the breeze carries the chaff away. Gideon is doing it somewhere else: down in a winepress, a pit for crushing grapes, out of sight. The text says why. He is hiding the wheat from the Midianites, who have been raiding the harvests until Israel is left with nothing. So here is a man, crouched in a hole, beating a little wheat by hand, listening for riders. And under the oak nearby, someone is sitting, watching him. An angel of the Lord. The first words out of the angel's mouth do not fit the scene at all.
screen: `THRESHING IN A WINEPRESS.` → `HIDING THE WHEAT.` → `SOMEONE UNDER THE OAK.`

segments.voice: The angel says: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Mighty. To a man in a hole. Gideon doesn't say thank you. He answers with a question, and it's a hard one. If the Lord is with us, why has all this happened to us? Where are all the wonders our fathers told us about, the ones from Egypt? It sounds like a complaint, and it is. Some rabbinic readers hear something else in it too: a man speaking up for his people, and they say that's part of why he was chosen. Then the Lord turns to him and says: go in this might of yours, and save Israel. Which might? So far, all Gideon has done is hide wheat and ask why. He says so himself. My family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. Notice what the answer is. Not a speech about his hidden talents. Just this: I will be with you. The strength comes with the promise. And notice what the angel never does. He never scolds the fear, or the question. He doesn't wait for Gideon to stop being scared before he calls him mighty. He calls him mighty while he's still hiding, and lets the name go ahead of him, the way a coat is held out before someone has stood up to put it on.
screen: `THE GREETING: MIGHTY MAN OF VALOR.` · `GIDEON ANSWERS WITH A QUESTION.` · `POOREST FAMILY, LEAST IN THE HOUSE.` · `THE ANSWER: I WILL BE WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THOU MIGHTY MAN OF VALOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see strength in someone who's scared. Settle in. Let one frightened person come to mind, someone you know who is scared of something right now, big or small. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. Then look for what they're already doing while they're scared. Getting up. Showing up. Keeping someone fed. Name it, silently, as strength. If you pray, you can hold the angel's first words over them: the Lord is with thee. The bell holds the time.
Mighty. What the angel calls Gideon while he's hiding wheat in a winepress, before he has done one brave thing. Today's word.
Your line: a coat held out first. Today, tell one scared person, in plain words, the strength you can see in them. Day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6:36–40)
718.hook: Gideon asks twice for a sign, and receives it
718.howItsDone: Jews read the fleece story in Judges 6 as part of the Former Prophets, and commentators debate whether Gideon's request was a forbidden test of God or a plea for reassurance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the angel under the oak. Your line was a coat held out first. Did you name the strength in someone scared? Today, the same mighty man, still not sure. Day seven hundred eighteen.

The armies of Midian have crossed over and camped in the valley of Jezreel. Gideon has blown the shofar, and men from several tribes are gathering behind him. Everything is moving. And Gideon goes out to the threshing floor with a piece of wool, a fleece, and lays it on the ground. He has already been told he'll save Israel. He has already seen fire leap from a rock to take his offering. And still he wants one more sign, and he asks for it to come down with the dew.
screen: `THE ARMIES GATHER.` → `A FLEECE ON THE THRESHING FLOOR.` → `ONE MORE SIGN.`

segments.voice: Here's what he asks. If there's dew on the fleece only, and the ground around it is dry, then I'll know you will save Israel by my hand, as you said. In the morning he gets up early and squeezes the fleece, and wrings out a bowl full of water. The ground is dry. That should be enough. It isn't. So he asks again, and listen to how he asks. "Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once." This time, reverse it: let the fleece be dry, and dew on all the ground. And that night, the text says, God did so. Dry wool, wet earth. Here is what the story leaves out: any anger. No rebuke, no lecture on faith. The sign is given, and given again, without a word of complaint. That matters, because the Torah also says not to put the Lord to the test. So readers argue over Gideon. Was he testing God, or asking for courage? Some say he was wrong to ask. Some say he wasn't asking about God at all; he was asking about himself, whether he was really the one. The story doesn't settle it. It just keeps the record: a frightened man doubted, said so out loud, politely, twice, and was answered both times.
screen: `DEW ON THE FLEECE, THE GROUND DRY.` · `LET NOT THINE ANGER BE HOT.` · `DRY FLEECE, WET GROUND.` · `NO REBUKE, BOTH TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: allow yourself your doubts. Settle, and let one honest doubt come up. About a decision, about yourself, about God, if that's where it lives. Don't argue it away, and don't scold it. Just name it plainly, the way Gideon did. Then breathe with it sitting next to you, as if it's allowed to be in the room. If you pray, you can bring it the way he did, with his opening words: let not thine anger be hot against me. And then the question. The bell holds the time.
Gideon's fleece. Wet when the ground was dry, then dry when the ground was wet: a doubter's sign, asked for twice and given twice. Today's word.
Your line: doubt is allowed. Today, when a doubt shows up, say it out loud to someone you trust instead of hiding it. Day seven hundred eighteen.

what it means: Gideon doubts out loud, politely, twice, and is answered both times without rebuke.

719.title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
719.hook: the army is cut to three hundred so no one thinks numbers won
719.howItsDone: Jews read Gideon's three hundred as part of studying Judges, and teachers often point to the stated reason for the cut: so that Israel would not say its own hand had saved it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's fleece, wet and then dry, asked for twice. Your line was doubt is allowed. Did you say one doubt out loud? Today, the army he gathered starts to shrink. Day seven hundred nineteen.

Thirty-two thousand men. That's the number the text gives for the army camped by the spring of Harod, with Midian spread out in the valley below. For a man who asked for sign after sign to believe he could win, it should be a comfort. Then the Lord speaks to Gideon, and the message is the last thing a nervous general wants to hear. Not: you need more. The opposite. The people that are with thee are too many.
screen: `THIRTY-TWO THOUSAND BY THE SPRING.` → `NOT TOO FEW.` → `TOO MANY.`

segments.voice: The reason is given straight out: "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." If the big army wins, everyone will credit the big army. So the cutting starts. First, whoever is fearful and trembling may go home. Twenty-two thousand leave. Ten thousand stay. Still too many. Gideon brings them down to the water, and the Lord sorts them by how they drink. Three hundred bring the water up in their hands and lap it. The rest kneel down to drink. The three hundred stay; everyone else goes home. The text never says why lapping was the test. Readers have guessed, and the story leaves it open; the point seems to be the cut, not the method. And then a tender detail. That night God tells Gideon to attack, and adds: if you're afraid to go down, take your servant Purah and go listen at the edge of the camp first. Even now, the fear is planned for. Gideon goes, and overhears a soldier telling a dream about a loaf of barley bread tumbling into the camp and flattening a tent. The battle itself is strange. The three hundred carry shofars, and torches hidden inside empty jars. They surround the camp, smash the jars, blow, and shout: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon." And they stand, each man in his place. The camp panics and flees. In the story, three hundred were enough, because the numbers were never what won.
screen: `TOO MANY, OR THEY'LL CREDIT THEMSELVES.` · `THE AFRAID GO HOME.` · `THREE HUNDRED WHO LAPPED.` · `JARS, TORCHES, SHOFARS: STAND IN PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing with less. Settle, and let your hands rest open and empty in your lap. Breathe. Then choose one thing today you'll do with less than you usually think you need. Fewer words in a message. One tab open instead of ten. One dish instead of three. Picture doing it, and notice that it's enough. If you pray, you can take the shout of the three hundred as a reminder of who gets the credit. The bell holds the time.
Three hundred. The ones left after the fearful went home and the rest were sorted at the water, cut down so no one could say their own hand saved them. Today's word.
Your line: fewer is enough. Today, do one ordinary job with less, and notice that it still gets done. Day seven hundred nineteen.

what it means: the army is cut down on purpose so that no one thinks numbers won the battle.

720.title: The bramble king (Judges 9:7–15)
720.hook: Jotham's fable: olive, fig and vine refuse to rule; only the bramble wants to
720.howItsDone: Jews study Jotham's fable in Judges 9 as part of the Former Prophets; it is often read alongside Gideon's refusal of kingship in Judges 8 when teachers discuss power and leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three hundred men with jars and torches. Your line was fewer is enough. What did you do with less? Today, Gideon is gone, and one of his sons wants to be king. Day seven hundred twenty.

A young man climbs to the top of Mount Gerizim and shouts down to the city of Shechem below. His name is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon. He's alive because he hid. His half-brother Abimelech has just murdered the rest of the brothers, and the men of Shechem have made Abimelech king. Jotham can't fight him. So he does something else. He tells them a story about trees. Hearken unto me, he calls down, that God may hearken unto you.
screen: `A VOICE FROM MOUNT GERIZIM.` → `ONE BROTHER ESCAPED.` → `A STORY ABOUT TREES.`

segments.voice: Once, the trees went out to anoint a king. They went to the olive tree: reign over us. And the olive said, should I give up my oil, that honors God and people, just to go and sway over the trees? They went to the fig: you reign. Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit? They went to the vine. Should I give up my wine, that cheers God and people? Each one has real work to do, and won't trade it for a crown. Last, the trees go to the bramble, a low thorny bush with no fruit worth picking. And the bramble says yes. Come and take shelter in my shade. Some readers smile at that: a bramble has almost no shade to give. Then, in the same breath, a threat: "and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon." So the fable says two things. The ones with something to give were too busy giving it. And the one with nothing to give wanted the crown most, and promised shelter while warning of fire. Jotham turns it on Shechem: if you've dealt honestly with my father's house, enjoy your king. If not, let fire come out of Abimelech and burn you, and fire come out of you and burn him. Then he runs. The rest of the chapter plays it out. In the end, Shechem and Abimelech turn on each other and both are destroyed, and the text says the curse of Jotham came upon them.
screen: `OLIVE, FIG AND VINE SAY NO.` · `THE BRAMBLE SAYS YES.` · `SHADE OFFERED, FIRE THREATENED.` · `THE CURSE COMES TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who is eager to rule. Settle, and bring to mind one group you belong to: a family, a team, a committee, a group chat. Who quietly bears fruit there, too busy to want charge of anything? Who wants the crown? Don't judge anyone; just notice. Then turn it gently on yourself. Where are you the olive tree, and where are you the bramble? Breathe with whatever you find. The bell holds the time.
bramble. The low thorny bush in Jotham's fable, the only tree with nothing to give that still said yes to the crown. Today's word.
Your line: the bramble wants the crown. Today, when someone pushes hard to be in charge, ask quietly what fruit they bear. Then ask the same of yourself. Day seven hundred twenty.

721.title: Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:29–40)
721.hook: a rash vow ends in tragedy, and the rabbis condemn it
721.howItsDone: Jews study Jephthah's vow with the Talmud and midrash beside the text; the rabbinic tradition treats the vow as rash and wrong, and Jewish law has ways for a vow to be released before a sage or court.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jotham's fable from the mountaintop. Your line was the bramble wants the crown. Did you notice who was eager to be in charge? Today, the end of the week, and a hard story. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Jephthah's brothers drove him out of the house; his mother wasn't their mother. Years later, with the Ammonites at war with Israel, the elders of Gilead come and ask him to lead them. He agrees. The spirit of the Lord comes upon him, the text says. He already has what he needs. And then, on the way to battle, he adds something nobody asked for. A vow. Whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace, shall be the Lord's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.
screen: `DRIVEN OUT, THEN CALLED BACK.` → `THE SPIRIT IS ALREADY ON HIM.` → `A VOW NOBODY ASKED FOR.`

segments.voice: He wins. He comes home to Mizpah. And out of the doors comes his daughter, dancing, with timbrels. The text stops to tell us: she was his only child. He tears his clothes. "I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back." She answers him with strange steadiness: do to me what you said. She asks for time to go up into the mountains with her friends and mourn, and he lets her go. When she returns, the text says only that he did with her according to his vow. And it adds that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament her. She is never named. The rabbis do not admire this. The Talmud names Jephthah among those who asked improperly: what if the thing that came out of the house had been unfit for an offering? A midrash goes further. The vow, it says, could have been released. Phinehas the priest was alive then. But Jephthah said, I'm the leader, why should I go to him? And Phinehas said, I'm the high priest, why should I go to him? Between two proud men, a girl was lost. Later commentators even differ on what happened to her: some read the verse as it sounds; some read it as a life set apart. Either way, the rabbis draw the same lesson. A promise made in a rush of feeling, to make sure of something already given, can cost what no one meant to pay.
